KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest surface analysis shows a surface trough
currently moving east across the Coastal Plain this morning 
with a slow moving cold front still well off to the west near 
the Appalachians. This cold front will take its time to get to 
ENC today but will likely weaken as it approaches which won't 
produce much change in the airmass across the area over the next
few days, but may help to focus shower and thunderstorm activity
along the seabreeze. As mentioned above, with a lack of airmass
change our area and much of the southeastern CONUS remains in 
the grip of a very hot and humid airmass. 

It is warm and muggy this morning with temps in the 70s to low 
80s. Much like yesterday, hot and humid conditions are once 
again expected today as temps climb into the mid 90s inland 
with upper 80s to low 90s along the immediate coast and OBX this
afternoon. However, unlike yesterday where there was little to 
no relief provided by convection, today will be a bit more 
active day and many areas could be convectively cooled by this 
evening. Still, at least some period of HI of 110-115F is 
likely especially along the seabreeze with widespread 105-110F 
values elsewhere. As a result have kept previously inherited 
Extreme Heat Warnings and Heat Advisories in place today 
starting at 11AM and continuing into 8PM tonight.

As we get into Wednesday and Thursday, aforementioned front 
will remain stalled along the coast. While cooler northeasterly 
flow will likely keep the most oppressive heat at bay from the 
Outer Banks to Albemarle Peninsula, areas south of US 264, and 
particularly south and west of US 70, will likely still see an 
elevated risk of HI between 105-110 each afternoon. A more 
widespread cooldown is likely Friday into the weekend as a 
stronger cold front nears.

KEY MESSAGE 2... Currently have a mid level shortwave moving 
through ENC this morning with associated surface trough pushing 
east towards the coast. We do have some ongoing shower and weak
thunderstorm activity noted along and north of Hwy 264
associated with this trough also pushing east. Outside of a 
stray gust to 40 mph, the main threat with these storms will be 
torrential downpours and frequent lightning. With a more stable 
airmass as you get closer to the coast and any leftover 
activity is forecast to weaken and eventually dissipate out near
the OBX and coastal waters near daybreak. 

Overall there will not be significant changes in the pattern 
into Thursday. Zonal flow will continue across the Mid-Atlantic
through Wednesday as an upper ridge remains centered to our 
south and an active northern stream jet remains to the north. 
This will change however on Thurs into Fri as upper level winds 
turn to a SW'rly direction out ahead of an incoming trough. At 
the mid levels, weak shortwaves will track across ENC daily, 
with the first of such moving across the area this afternoon and
evening, and another shortwave pushing through Wed afternoon. 
At the surface, the aforementioned front eventually stalls near 
the coast and combined with an inland moving seabreeze, this 
will be the focal point for shower and thunderstorm activity 
today and tomorrow. Main corridor today for shower and 
thunderstorm activity looks to be along Hwy 17 corridor and 
points east with just isolated chances further to the west. As 
we get into tomorrow, this threat likely pushes further inland 
with the seabreeze as the afternoon wears on. Precip chances 
generally remain around 20-40% each afternoon and evening before
chances decrease after sunset. Despite poor shear, high PWATs 
exceeding 2.25" are expected and a stronger cell could pose an 
isolated wet microburst threat this afternoon and tomorrow. 
Otherwise, overall severe threat is low - less than 5%.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Deeper trough begins to dig across the Ohio
River Valley on Thursday and push towards the Eastern Seaboard 
on Fri and into the weekend. Stronger shortwave will also be 
transiting along this trough bringing a stronger cold front to 
ENC this weekend, though latest trends suggest as this front 
nears the area it also will stall and weaken. Either way this 
front will bring a much welcome pattern change serving to both 
offer a reprieve from oppressive heat and humidity and a chance 
of strong to severe thunderstorms as shear increases alongside 
the boundary with stronger troughing. Details are coming into 
better focus but there are still some details to hammer out in 
the coming days such as frontal timing and strength. Will 
continue to monitor trends in the forecast for any adjustments 
in the coming days. NCAR medium- range AI NWP guidance continues
to suggest at least modest probabilities (around 5%) of an 
environment favorable for strong to severe convection.
